label: November–December 1880
atlas_dek: The episodes reported from November through December 1880 in our dossiers that involve anti-Black violence or threats, placed on 1910 county lines and by month (some events were first reported the month after). Lynchings of white victims and others, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers but not on the map. Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 64 episodes reported from November through December 1880. As in 1881 and 1882, this collection covers two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white victims and others, and the many lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers; only the anti-Black episodes are on the map. November opened with the presidential election, and much of the month’s violence came with it: Red Shirts holding the polls at Darlington, South Carolina, at gunpoint, election-day riots at Edgefield, Johnston and Sumter, and Black voters driven from the polls. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later, and from searches for victims in the Monroe Work Today inventory that the month runs missed. The search used white papers only: American Stories and the other Chronicling America pages, and, new with these months, pages from four state digital-newspaper programs (Georgia, Pennsylvania, Nebraska and Oregon) that neither holds. These pages, most of them Georgia papers such as the Savannah Morning News and the Columbus dailies, added six episodes and new reports of eleven others. The rest of 1880, January to October, is still to come; the July and August 1880 dossiers from our August series will join this collection when those months are run.

We wrote 82 dossiers; 18 are set aside, and 21 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope. Set aside: four duplicates; a November report recalling two lynchings from earlier in 1880, held for those months; anti-Black-scope events in which no report gives anyone’s race and no lynching was involved (eight); an event with no force; a night shooting by one man with no racial element found; a cannon said to have been aimed at voters, reported only as hearsay; and a threatened lynching of a Black man by a Black crowd.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals. An attack by one private person counts when it has racial content or context, such as a whipping over an alleged insult to a white woman or an ambush of Black families; a quarrel that happens to cross the color line is set aside.

Method: a research agent searched the papers; for these months it was OpenAI’s Codex or Google’s Gemini. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom, and what the reports suggest lay behind a killing; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.
